issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession on title must establish that the title document covers the specific property claimed.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of three rooms based on a court-auction sale certificate issued to their predecessor.
The certificate described a house by division and serial number and gave boundaries, but did not identify the claimed rooms as part of that house.
The schedule said to describe the suit property was absent from the record, and the alleged municipal statement supporting the plaintiffs’ claim was not proved.
The trial and appellate courts found that the certificate did not connect the property it covered with the claimed rooms.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish title to the suit rooms, and the concurrent factual finding was not shown to be illegal or liable to interference in second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A claimant relying on a title document must prove that it relates to the specific property claimed; a factual finding based on relevant evidence is not displaced merely by assertion on second appeal. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiffs brought a suit seeking possession on the basis of claimed title.
predicates.only_title_document_is_sale_certificate: The plaintiffs relied on a sale certificate as their only evidence supporting title.
predicates.certificate_does_not_identify_claimed_pr: The sale certificate did not connect the property it described with the specific rooms for which possession was sought.

issues.definition: When a possession suit rests on title and the only title document does not identify the property claimed, the claimant’s title is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A final civil appellate decision between the parties on whether a tenancy existed cannot be reopened in a later suit raising that same issue.
material_facts: In an earlier possession suit following termination of an alleged tenancy, the civil appellate court held that it could reconsider the tenancy question despite the rent authorities’ contrary finding.
That appellate court concluded that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties.
The decision was not challenged further and became final between the parties.
The plaintiffs later brought a suit based on title, treating the occupants as persons in unauthorised occupation, and the tenancy issue was raised again.
issues.conclusion: The final civil appellate decision that no landlord-tenant relationship existed was binding between the parties and could not be reopened in the later suit; the Court did not need to decide whether the rent authorities’ finding was independently binding.
issues.legal_principle: A final adjudication between the same parties on an issue operates as res judicata in later proceedings on that issue. The judgment discussed Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act in describing the earlier suit and noted the argument based on Pralhad Lanchad Chavan v. Iqbal Hussain Inayat Hussain Badri, 1996 (5) SCC 428, but expressly found it unnecessary to decide that argument. The binding effect here arose from the final civil appellate decision in the earlier proceedings.

rule.if: later_civil_suit_between_same_parties and prior_final_civil_appeal_decided_tenancy_status and prior_decision_not_challenged and same_tenancy_issue_raised_again

predicates.later_civil_suit_between_same_parties: The same parties brought a later civil suit after an earlier civil proceeding.
predicates.prior_final_civil_appeal_decided_tenancy: A civil appellate court in the earlier proceeding decided whether a tenancy existed between the parties.
predicates.prior_decision_not_challenged: The parties did not challenge the earlier appellate decision further, and it became final between them.
predicates.same_tenancy_issue_raised_again: The tenancy question decided in the earlier appeal was raised again in the later suit.

issues.definition: When the same parties bring a later civil suit, an unchallenged final civil appellate decision on the tenancy issue prevents that issue from being reopened.

issues.legal_issue: Continuous possession of property as owner, adverse to the claimant, for the required period can perfect title by adverse possession.
material_facts: The trial and first appellate courts found that the defendants’ predecessor had possessed the suit rooms continuously for more than thirty years before the suit.
Those courts found that he occupied the rooms in his own right and was in adverse possession against the plaintiffs’ predecessor.

The alleged statements by the predecessor acknowledging the plaintiffs’ predecessor as landlord were not legally proved; the declarant was deceased, and the statements were not proved under Section 32 of the Evidence Act.
issues.conclusion: The defendants’ predecessor had perfected title to the suit rooms by adverse possession, and the concurrent finding was sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession may perfect title when possession is continuous, hostile to the claimant, and maintained as one’s own for the required period. The Court applied that principle to the concurrent finding of possession for more than thirty years. It also rejected the alleged statements acknowledging the claimant’s title because they were not proved, including under Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: possession_suit and continuous_possession_as_owner and possession_adverse_to_claimant and possession_exceeds_required_period

predicates.possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.continuous_possession_as_owner: The opposing possessor continuously occupied the property in their own right as owner.
predicates.possession_adverse_to_claimant: The possessor’s occupation was adverse to the claimant’s asserted ownership.
predicates.possession_exceeds_required_period: The possessor remained in adverse possession for longer than the period required to perfect title.

issues.definition: In a possession suit, continuous occupation as owner, adverse to the claimant and lasting longer than the required period, results in title being perfected by adverse possession.
